principles: Treat every locale as an original editorial article, not a sentence-by-sentence translation.
Preserve the dramatic argument built around Macbeth Act 2 Scene 2 and Hamlet Act 4 Scene 5, using standard local play titles and character names.
Use each locale’s established theatre terminology for stage directions, dialogue, captions and Deaf/hard-of-hearing audiences.

Translate generic captions, captioning, subtitles and stage-directions terminology into natural local-language equivalents; keep English only for quoted Shakespeare wording, established product names and official organization names.

Keep product behavior exact: Accessibility Caption is a manual Editor line type; it has no speaker; it survives Skip Stage Directions; simulations, projections and audience views render one bracket pair; already-bracketed text is not double-wrapped; script analysis does not infer this type.
In the English source, use the official UI label Hide Character Names, never Skip Character Names. Localized articles should use the official label from that locale’s UI.
Use the supplied Macbeth text excerpt and the supplied editor recording as inline images; use the latest supplied black Cockpit screenshot as the hero image.
Do not imply that every stage direction should become a caption. The editorial question is whether missing the sound removes information needed to understand the moment.
Do not turn sound captioning into visual description; visible movement is a different access need.

Keep English source phrases such as Knocking within, Knock within and A noise within only where discussing Shakespeare’s source text; localize surrounding explanation, including link labels for resource titles where a descriptive translation is clearer.
Traditional Chinese is an approved preserved translation and must not be regenerated from the English source without explicit instruction.
